focus.title: Maintain the largest-so-far rule
focus.code: int maximum(const std::vector<int>& v){ int best=v.at(0); for(std::size_t i=1;i<v.size();++i) if(v[i]>best) best=v[i]; return best; }
explain: const vector<int>& v borrows the caller’s vector without modifying it. at(0) checks the first index. The loop starts at 1, uses < to stop before size(), increments i, and replaces best only when the next value is larger. return sends the answer back.
focus.what: After each completed iteration, best is the maximum of the values visited so far.
focus.where: The function is defined before main calls it. The scan itself runs at execution time.
focus.why: One pass is enough; sorting would do extra work and change the input order.
focus.invariant: The input must be nonempty for a successful result. best must be a value from the visited prefix.
focus.risk: Starting best at zero gives a wrong result for all-negative input. Replacing < with <= reads beyond the vector at the last iteration.

focus.title: Check the example trace
explain: The brace list constructs a temporary vector from 4, 9, 2, 7. It stays alive through this call, so the borrowed const reference is valid. The returned integer is sent to cout, then a newline.
focus.what: The trace is best=4, then 9, then 9, then 9.
focus.where: The temporary input is destroyed after the full expression finishes.
focus.why: This small fixture makes the scan’s invariant easy to check before using larger inputs.
focus.invariant: The final output is 9. The function returns an integer value, not a reference to a temporary.
focus.risk: Returning a reference to a local best would produce a dangling reference once the function returns.
